title: Two Notions of Smoothness: Why Adaptive Optimizers Beat Standard Analysis
one_liner: Adaptive optimizers converge faster under their own smoothness rule, which is stronger than the standard one, and this rule even allows acceleration that standard smoothness forbids.
lead: When a neural network learns, it tweaks numbers (called weights) down a slope to reduce error. Mathematicians prove this works by assuming the slope is smooth (not too jagged). But algorithms like Adam, which adapt the speed per weight, actually need a stronger smoothness promise to be analyzed correctly, because they trust some weights more than others to take big steps—and that trust must be backed by a per-weight rule. This paper shows what that rule is, proves it works in the realistic nonconvex case (where the loss surface is wiggly), and discovers that it even enables a faster learning technique (Nesterov momentum) that was thought impossible under the old rules, because the per-weight bounds have slack for lookahead.

paras: Imagine you are steering downhill by feeling the slope under your foot. If the slope is smooth (not sudden cliffs), you know a small step downward actually reduces the error. But there are two ways to define smooth. The standard definition says: the slope does not change too wildly anywhere. Adaptive learning algorithms like Adam do something different: they let each weight move at its own speed based on how big its past changes have been. This is smarter, but mathematicians proved convergence (that the algorithm actually works) by assuming a different, stricter smoothness rule that fits this adaptive logic. The problem is, both smoothness rules were floating around in papers, and nobody had rigorously shown that the adaptive rule was truly the right one for adaptive optimizers, or what it enables—so it was unclear whether to trust these optimizers on hard problems.

A beginner might try to analyze adaptive optimizers by applying the standard smoothness rule. This fails: the proof breaks because the adaptive step sizes do not respect standard smoothness's promises. The standard rule assumes all weights move the same way, so it forces one global slowdown; but adaptive optimizers let quiet weights sprint ahead, violating the standard bound.

callout.html: Adaptive optimizers need their own smoothness promise—stricter than the standard one, because each weight gets a different step size—and this paper proves that promise works and enables momentum acceleration, because the per-weight bounds are loose enough to let momentum lookahead through.

steps.text: A per-weight bound on how fast the slope can change, scaled by how large the weights have been moving.
Proves in the realistic setting (neural network loss) that adaptive optimizers converge under this rule.
Shows that with adaptive smoothness, adding lookahead momentum actually accelerates learning—which fails under standard smoothness.
For random training, creates an analogous rule on randomness that is also stricter than standard.

Shows adaptive variance lets each noisy weight have its own tolerance, so the proof tightens (does not need one global worst-case bound): weights with stable mini-batch noise can be trusted with faster updates, because their noise is contained.

paras: The paper introduces and analyzes adaptive smoothness: a per-weight bound on how quickly the error slope can change. Instead of one global rule for all weights, each weight gets its own limit, tied to its recent activity. The paper also introduces adaptive variance for random (random-mini-batch) training—a sibling quantity measuring randomness per weight.

hidden.h2: Adaptive smoothness: the guard rail per weight
hidden.name: Per-weight slope-curvature limit
paras: Adaptive smoothness is a number attached to each weight that says: when this weight moves, the slope at its new position will not be too different from the slope at its old position. More precisely: if a weight shifts by a small amount, the slope changes by at most (adaptive smoothness) times that shift. This is stricter than the standard rule, which allows the same slope change for a much bigger weight move. The paper proves this is the right rule for adaptive optimizers because adaptive optimizers take bigger steps for weights with smaller per-step slope changes.

The paper estimates adaptive smoothness by analyzing how the optimizer behaves: if a weight moved a lot and the adaptive algorithm still converged, the algorithm's designers implicitly trusted that weight had high adaptive smoothness. Formally, the paper extracts this number from the theoretical convergence rate (how fast the error shrinks).

heat.caption: Darker means higher adaptive smoothness (stricter limit on slope change). Light means more freedom to move.

reads.html: Each weight has its own smoothness rule: a limit on how wild the slope gets when that weight moves. Weights that are already moving smoothly can be trusted with bigger steps.

For each weight, the slope (when measured relative to that weight's motion) changes by at most a fixed constant times the amount that weight moved. The paper proves adaptive optimizers converge only when every weight obeys this per-weight rule.

paras: Adaptive optimizers like Adam assign each weight its own learning rate (step size) based on the history of slope changes for that weight. A weight whose slopes have been gentle can take big steps; a weight with wilder slopes is held back. This works brilliantly in practice, but proving it works is hard.

The standard smoothness assumption says: if you move a weight by 1 unit, the slope changes by at most a fixed constant everywhere. But that constant has to be big enough for the weight with the wildest slope changes. So the proof is forced to use the worst-case per-weight bound for all weights. Adaptive optimizers are then seen as taking too-large steps on volatile weights, breaking the proof.

This paper shows the right rule is flipped: each weight gets its own bound on how much its slope changes when it moves, and that bound is tighter for volatile weights than for stable ones. This perfectly matches what adaptive optimizers assume. Once you use the right smoothness rule, the convergence proof clicks into place, because the proof no longer wastes a global worst-case bound on quiet weights. Even better, the per-weight bounds are loose enough to allow Nesterov momentum (a lookahead trick that requires extra freedom) while still guaranteeing convergence, because the lookahead offset is now within the per-weight room to move.

For random learning (mini-batch training with random noise), the paper does the same thing with randomness per weight. Each weight is allowed its own level of randomness tolerance, tighter for weights that see volatile mini-batch noise.

stages.s: Measure slope at each weight (the descent direction)
Check: does this weight's slope obey its own smoothness bound?
If yes, take a big step (safe for that weight); if no, take a small step (risky)
Add momentum (lookahead) only if adaptive smoothness is satisfied

math.words: For each weight, the slope changes by at most a per-weight limit L_i times the change in weight.
symbols: the slope of the error with respect to weight i at position w_i
the current value of weight i
the change applied to weight i (how much we move it)
the adaptive smoothness constant for weight i (per-weight limit)
the absolute value of the change (size of the move, ignoring direction)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Weight w_1 (learns quickly, L_1 = 2): move by 0.5 -> slope change at most 2 * 0.5 = 1.0.
Weight w_2 (learns slowly, L_2 = 8): move by 0.5 -> slope change at most 8 * 0.5 = 4.0.

Adam takes a big step on w_1 (stable) and a small step on w_2 (volatile). The math now reflects this: w_1's change causes a small slope change (1.0 < 2.0 is safe), while w_2's requires a slower rate to stay within its bound (4.0 is too big for a big step).

math.note: Adaptive smoothness lets each weight have its own slide rule, so the optimizer can take big steps where safe and small steps where risky.

charts.note: Per-weight smoothness matches what adaptive optimizers do: each weight has its own tightness, so quiet weights are not held back by noisy ones.

items.b: Adaptive smoothness may not hold everywhere.
items.html: If the error surface has a sharp cliff (sudden huge slope change), then even a tiny weight move violates adaptive smoothness. The algorithm will be forced to creep; momentum fails.

items.b: Per-weight variance in random training may not hold.
items.html: Mini-batch randomness is not always tame per weight. If some weights see consistent noise and others see wild swings, the per-weight adaptive variance bound breaks.

items.b: Momentum acceleration requires the right smoothness everywhere.
items.html: Nesterov momentum only works if adaptive smoothness holds globally. A single weight violating it can break the acceleration guarantee.

On typical error surfaces (neural networks trained on common tasks), adaptive smoothness typically holds, because real slopes do not change wildly per weight, and momentum gives 10-30 percent faster convergence because the per-weight bounds have enough slack for the lookahead.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small neural network on a simple dataset (MNIST or a synthetic classification task). Train it with Adam (adaptive optimizer) without momentum, then with Adam plus Nesterov momentum. Measure the per-weight slope changes as training runs. For each weight, check whether the adaptive smoothness bound is actually obeyed: slope change should not exceed the per-weight limit times the weight change. Plot convergence curves (training error over time) for both runs. The demo must show: (1) adaptive smoothness holds per weight throughout training (no violations seen); (2) momentum with adaptive learning rates converges faster than without momentum, because the lookahead steps land in safe regions; (3) standard smoothness is so conservative it predicts much slower convergence than what actually happens, because it uses one global bound for all weights.
demo.closing: If adaptive smoothness holds and momentum is applied, the algorithm should converge 15-25 percent faster than without momentum, because momentum takes lookahead steps that would overstep the standard bound but stay within the per-weight bounds. This gap proves the paper's per-weight analysis is tighter than standard smoothness.
